label: Meteorology (forecast and warning operations)
description: A weather forecast and warning team: a forecast office, a broadcast weather team or a meteorologist embedded with emergency management or a utility. They watch radar, satellite, soundings and model guidance, issue watches, warnings and decision-support briefings, and work with emergency managers, broadcasters and the public. Plans and doctrine: NWS directives for warning products, the integrated warning team practice and, for hurricanes, the hurricane evacuation studies and decision timeline. Products here are exercise products, never operational ones.

vocabulary.facility: the forecast office and its warning operations floor
vocabulary.public: residents, spotters, emergency managers and broadcast viewers
vocabulary.frontline: warning forecasters, mesoanalysts, decision support meteorologists, on-air meteorologists
vocabulary.operationsCenter: the warning operations floor of the forecast office

it: public website and social media accounts
product dissemination and the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters
the station's weather app and push alerts (broadcast team)
ot: WSR-88D radar (dual polarization) sites and their communications
model guidance (HRRR, NAM, GFS and ensembles)
backup power and generator at the office and radar sites

roles.name: Lead Forecaster / Shift Supervisor
roles.description: Owns staffing and sectorization, who warns which counties, when to call in help and service backup.

roles.name: Warning Forecaster (radar sector)
roles.description: Issues and updates tornado, severe thunderstorm and flash flood warnings and statements.

roles.name: Mesoanalyst
roles.description: Watches the environment (surface, upper air, satellite, mesoanalysis) and advises the warning forecasters.

roles.name: Decision Support (IDSS) Meteorologist
roles.description: Briefs emergency managers and partners, answers their questions and joins their calls.

roles.name: Warning Coordination Meteorologist
roles.description: Owns partner and media relations, the social media presence and the decision support program.

roles.name: Hydrologist
roles.description: Owns river and flash flood forecasts with the River Forecast Center.

roles.name: Science and Operations Officer
roles.description: Owns science, training and the post-event review.

roles.name: Meteorologist in Charge
roles.description: Owns office decisions, continuity and external escalation.

roles.name: Communications / Social Media Forecaster
roles.description: Owns graphics, posts, partner chat and spotter coordination.

roles.name: Chief Meteorologist
roles.description: Owns the on-air forecast, the station's severe weather coverage and what the team says is certain.

roles.name: On-Air Meteorologist
roles.description: Presents the forecast and warnings live and interprets radar for viewers.

roles.name: Weather Producer
roles.description: Owns the weather show rundown, graphics and the link between the weather desk and the newsroom.

roles.name: Digital and Social Producer
roles.description: Owns the app alerts, the website and social posts, and corrects rumors.

roles.name: News Director
roles.description: Decides wall-to-wall coverage, cut-ins and staffing outside the weather team.

roles.name: Embedded Meteorologist (emergency management or utility)
roles.description: Briefs the emergency manager or the utility's operations leaders on what the weather will do to their decisions.

roles.name: County Emergency Manager
roles.description: Decides sirens, shelters, evacuations and the county's own messages from the forecast office's products.

roles.name: Public Information Officer
roles.description: Owns the public message so it matches the warning products.

outsideParties: SKYWARN spotters and amateur radio operators
large event venues and venue operators
mediaChannels: the forecast office's social media accounts
a viral post with a photo of a funnel cloud
a county emergency management Facebook page

addedThreatFamilies.label: Convective outbreak (severe thunderstorms and tornadoes)
addedThreatFamilies.description: A day of organized severe thunderstorms worked from the morning outlook through watches, warnings, reports and the storm survey.

phaseArc.title: Outlook
phaseArc.goal: The team sees the setup coming and must decide how loudly to say so.
beats: A convective outlook raises the risk category for the area
A model run disagrees with the previous one on storm mode
A partner asks whether to staff up for tomorrow

phaseArc.title: Environment
phaseArc.goal: Assess whether the atmosphere will support storms: instability, shear, capping, and where storms will form first.
beats: A morning sounding shows a strong cap and rich low-level moisture
A mesoanalysis shows a boundary lifting north
A mesoscale discussion says a watch is likely soon

phaseArc.title: Watch
phaseArc.goal: A watch is out. Partners decide posture before anything has formed.
beats: A tornado watch is issued for the area
Emergency managers ask what the watch changes for them
The first storm initiates on the boundary and the radar shows it organizing

phaseArc.title: Warnings
phaseArc.goal: Warning decisions under time pressure with incomplete radar evidence, balancing lead time against false alarms.
beats: A rotating storm approaches a town and the warning forecaster must choose the polygon and the damage threat tag
Two storms need warnings at once and one forecaster is covering both
A spotter report conflicts with radar
A partner asks for a conference call mid-warning

phaseArc.title: Reports and verification
phaseArc.goal: Reports arrive and the team separates confirmed damage from rumor, updating products and partners.
beats: Local storm reports and a damage photo arrive
A viral photo of a funnel cloud is from another year
A county emergency manager asks for an impact statement

phaseArc.title: Survey and recovery
phaseArc.goal: Damage survey, public information statement and the review of how the warnings did.
beats: A damage survey team is dispatched and the rating process begins
A resident criticizes a late siren
The office compares warning times with the first reports

decisionPointExamples: Whether to call in extra staff before the first storm forms
Whether to issue a tornado warning on a radar-indicated circulation with no spotter confirmation
Whether to add the highest damage threat tag, with the cost of warning fatigue if it is wrong
How to split warning responsibility when two storms need warnings at once
Whether to join a partner call during a warning
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: Radar signatures, soundings, mesoanalysis parameters, spotter and public reports, and partner questions that show what the storm is doing and whether the evidence is enough to warn.
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: A radar outage or a dissemination failure in the middle of the warning window; a spotter network that goes quiet; a county siren system that cannot be activated.
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: County and municipal emergency management, the 911 center, SKYWARN spotters, broadcast partners and neighboring forecast offices.
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: The setup and the warnings must follow the real product sequence: outlook, then mesoscale discussion, then watch, then warnings and statements, then local storm reports and a public information statement. Use exact times and the product header conventions, never invent a watch number that contradicts the documents, and keep every product marked as an exercise.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Flash flood (heavy rain)
addedThreatFamilies.description: Heavy rain on saturated or urban ground that floods fast, worked as rainfall forecasts, gauge and radar rainfall estimates, warnings and rescues.

phaseArc.title: Outlook
phaseArc.goal: The excessive rainfall outlook and the river forecast frame the risk before the rain starts.
beats: An excessive rainfall outlook shows a Slight or Moderate risk
The river forecast center and the office disagree on soil moisture
A partner asks about road closure planning

phaseArc.title: Heavy rain begins
phaseArc.goal: Rain rates climb and the first gauges respond.
beats: Radar estimates show rain rates over two inches an hour
A stream gauge begins rising
A flood watch is already in effect

phaseArc.title: Warnings
phaseArc.goal: The flash flood warning decision with reports of water on roads.
beats: Storms train over the same area
A flash flood warning is issued with an impact tag
A 911 center reports a water rescue

phaseArc.title: Emergency
phaseArc.goal: Flooding is severe enough that the highest level of flash flood warning is considered.
beats: A report of homes and vehicles flooded and people trapped
The office debates a flash flood emergency
A reservoir or levee concern is raised

phaseArc.title: Recovery
phaseArc.goal: Reports, river crests, road closures and the review.
beats: Gauges crest and fall
A public information statement summarizes rainfall and flooding
Residents ask why the warning came after the water

decisionPointExamples: Whether to issue a flash flood emergency, with the cost of lost credibility if the impact is smaller
Whether to extend a warning in time or let it expire and reissue
How to word the call to action for drivers
Whether to ask the emergency manager to close a low-water crossing
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: Rainfall rate estimates, gauge trends, rescue calls and photographs of water over roads.
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: A gauge that stops reporting; a radar beam blocked in the hills; conflicting rainfall estimates.
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: County emergency management, 911, the river forecast center, road and highway departments and dam or reservoir operators.
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Use rainfall in inches over stated hours, gauge stage and flood stage in feet, and keep warnings for flash floods separate from river flood warnings. Reports must come from named gauges, counties and roads in the documents.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Tropical cyclone (hurricane)
addedThreatFamilies.description: A tropical storm or hurricane approaching a coast, worked as advisories, watches and warnings, surge, evacuation decisions and landfall.

phaseArc.title: Formation and outlook
phaseArc.goal: A disturbance becomes a named storm and the first advisories raise questions for the coast.
beats: The National Hurricane Center issues its first advisory
A forecast cone includes the county
Emergency management asks for a decision timeline

phaseArc.title: Watches
phaseArc.goal: Hurricane and storm surge watches begin the clock for evacuations.
beats: A hurricane watch is issued about 48 hours before tropical-storm-force winds are expected
The county compares evacuation clearance times with the wind arrival time
Models disagree on the track

phaseArc.title: Warnings and evacuation
phaseArc.goal: Warnings begin; decisions about evacuation, shelters and closures have to be made before the winds arrive.
beats: A hurricane warning is issued about 36 hours before tropical-storm-force winds
The emergency manager must decide on evacuation zones
The storm intensifies faster than forecast

phaseArc.title: Landfall
phaseArc.goal: Winds, surge and rain arrive and the team shifts to current conditions and rescue support.
beats: Tropical-storm-force winds arrive
Surge flooding is reported earlier than expected
Power and communications fail in parts of the area

phaseArc.title: Aftermath
phaseArc.goal: Damage assessment, public information and the review of the forecast.
beats: Reports of surge height and wind damage arrive
Residents who stayed ask for help
The office and the county review the decision timeline

decisionPointExamples: When to order evacuation of each zone given its clearance time and the forecast arrival of tropical-storm-force winds
Whether to keep a shelter open as the track shifts
Whether to close a bridge before sustained winds reach the closure threshold
Whether to staff the office around the clock and cancel leave
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: Advisory updates, hurricane hunter data, forecast model tracks and surge guidance that change the decision timeline.
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: A power failure at the emergency operations center; communication loss with the shelter; a traffic jam that slows evacuation.
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: The National Hurricane Center, state and county emergency management, and shelter operators.
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Use advisory numbers, issuance times at the standard advisory hours, wind speeds as the product states them, and the watch and warning lead times of the storm products. The decision timeline is: evacuation start equals the arrival of tropical-storm-force winds minus the clearance time.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Winter storm
addedThreatFamilies.description: Snow, ice or blizzard conditions that affect roads, power and operations, worked as forecast discussions, warnings and impact briefings.

phaseArc.title: Forecast
phaseArc.goal: Uncertain snow and ice amounts must be communicated before the storm.
beats: A winter storm watch is issued
Models disagree on the rain-snow line
Road agencies ask for the likeliest and the worst case

phaseArc.title: Onset
phaseArc.goal: The first impacts appear and the forecast is tested against observations.
beats: Temperatures stay above freezing longer than forecast
A winter storm warning is issued
The first crashes are reported

phaseArc.title: Peak
phaseArc.goal: Snow rates, ice accumulation or wind peak and operations are disrupted.
beats: Freezing rain brings down trees and lines
Blizzard conditions close a highway
Power outages rise

phaseArc.title: Recovery
phaseArc.goal: Amounts are verified and the next phase of cold is handled.
beats: Snowfall reports arrive
Wind chills drop overnight
The public asks why the forecast amount was off

decisionPointExamples: Whether to upgrade a watch to a warning given forecast uncertainty
Whether to recommend closing schools or delaying a shift
How to describe the ice accumulation range to the power utility
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: Observed temperatures, precipitation types and amounts, webcam and road reports.
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: A road weather sensor outage; a power outage at a spotter site; a forecast graphic posted with the wrong amounts.
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: Road and highway agencies, utilities, school districts and emergency management.
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Use inches of snow and hundredths of an inch of ice, product names and times in local time, and keep advisory, warning and watch language separate.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Extreme heat
addedThreatFamilies.description: A multi-day heat wave that stresses people and power, worked as forecasts, heat products and public health coordination.

phaseArc.title: Forecast
phaseArc.goal: The heat is forecast several days out and partners plan.
beats: An extreme heat watch is issued
The power utility asks for peak temperatures
A health department asks about cooling centers

phaseArc.title: Onset
phaseArc.goal: The first hot days begin and the first illnesses are reported.
beats: A heat advisory is issued
Hospital visits begin to rise
An outdoor event asks about continuing

phaseArc.title: Peak
phaseArc.goal: Heat and humidity peak with warm nights and strained infrastructure.
beats: Overnight lows stay high
The grid operator warns of tight supply
A cooling center runs out of space

phaseArc.title: Recovery
phaseArc.goal: Heat ends and the review begins.
beats: Temperatures fall
The health department counts cases
The office reviews its messaging

decisionPointExamples: Whether to upgrade a heat advisory to a warning for a vulnerable population
Whether to recommend canceling an outdoor event
Whether to ask partners to open cooling centers overnight
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: Temperature and heat index observations, overnight lows, hospital and cooling center counts.
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: A sensor reading too high from a bad exposure; a power outage at a cooling center.
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: Public health, the electric utility and grid operator, school districts and event organizers.
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Use heat index and temperature in degrees Fahrenheit with the stated thresholds of the local office, and mention warm overnight lows.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Fire weather
addedThreatFamilies.description: Dry, windy conditions that raise fire danger, worked as fire weather forecasts, red flag warnings and spot forecasts for an active fire.

phaseArc.title: Forecast
phaseArc.goal: The fire weather forecast shows critical conditions coming.
beats: A fire weather watch is issued
Fuel moisture is below average
Land managers ask about burn permits

phaseArc.title: Red flag
phaseArc.goal: Warnings are in effect and a fire starts.
beats: A red flag warning is issued
Wind gusts exceed the criteria
A fire starts and a spot forecast is requested

phaseArc.title: Active fire
phaseArc.goal: Weather drives the fire's behavior and decisions.
beats: A wind shift is forecast for the afternoon
Dry thunderstorms bring new starts
Smoke affects aviation and air quality

phaseArc.title: Recovery
phaseArc.goal: Weather eases and the review begins.
beats: Humidity rises overnight
Fire officials ask for a spot forecast update
The review compares the forecast with observed winds

decisionPointExamples: Whether to issue a red flag warning for an area where fuel conditions are borderline
How to word a spot forecast for a wind shift that affects firefighter safety
Whether to brief the incident commander in person
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: Observed winds, humidity and temperature at nearby stations, smoke reports and fire behavior reports.
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: A weather station down near the fire; a data outage for the spot forecast request form.
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: Fire agencies, land managers, incident management teams and utilities.
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Use sustained winds and gusts in miles per hour, relative humidity in percent and the criteria of the local fire weather plan.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Aviation weather
addedThreatFamilies.description: Thunderstorms, low ceilings, wind shear or ice that disrupts flights, worked as METARs, TAFs, advisories and traffic management decisions.

phaseArc.title: Forecast
phaseArc.goal: The terminal forecast shows storms or low ceilings.
beats: A TAF forecasts thunderstorms with a probability group
Airlines ask about the timing
A convective advisory is issued for the area

phaseArc.title: Onset
phaseArc.goal: Conditions begin to degrade at the airport.
beats: A METAR shows reduced visibility and a thunderstorm
Ramp operations stop for lightning
A ground stop is considered

phaseArc.title: Disruption
phaseArc.goal: Operations are limited and decisions about the TAF are needed.
beats: The TAF needs an amendment
A ground stop is issued
Crosswinds exceed limits on the main runway

phaseArc.title: Recovery
phaseArc.goal: Weather improves and the backlog clears.
beats: Visibility improves
Departures resume
The airport reviews its lightning procedures

decisionPointExamples: Whether to amend a TAF now or wait for confirmation
Whether to recommend a ground stop to traffic management
Whether to stop ramp operations for lightning within the stated radius
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: Surface observations, radar lightning and echo tops, pilot reports.
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: An automated observation system fault; a missing observation in the TAF period.
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: Air traffic control, airlines and airport operations, and the center weather service unit.
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Use the METAR and TAF formats exactly, with valid times in UTC, standard weather codes and cloud heights in hundreds of feet.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Weather service degradation
addedThreatFamilies.description: The forecasting or warning service itself is impaired: radar outage, data or dissemination failure, office evacuation and backup, staffing shortfall or misinformation.

phaseArc.title: Degradation
phaseArc.goal: A system or staffing problem is noticed while weather is a concern.
beats: The radar site stops updating
Staffing falls below the planned level for the shift
A product transmission fails

phaseArc.title: Workaround
phaseArc.goal: The team must invoke backup procedures and tell partners.
beats: A neighboring office is asked to provide service backup
Partners are told what products they can expect
The team chooses between two radars farther away

phaseArc.title: Decision
phaseArc.goal: The weather worsens while the problem persists.
beats: A tornado-producing storm approaches the gap in coverage
A decision is needed whether to issue warnings from partial data
A false warning spreads on social media

phaseArc.title: Recovery
phaseArc.goal: Service is restored and the team reviews.
beats: The system returns with a data gap
The backup office hands back
The review lists what partners experienced

decisionPointExamples: Whether to ask a neighboring office to take over warning responsibility
Whether to warn on partial radar data
Whether to publicly state that radar coverage is limited
Whether to evacuate the office and where to relocate
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: System alarms, product transmission logs, partner questions and gaps in the data feed.
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: A backup circuit that fails; a handoff that loses context; a vendor that cannot restore until morning.
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: Neighboring forecast offices, the regional headquarters, the radar operations center and emergency management.
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Describe outages by the system affected and the products that stop, not by vendor. Always state what partners can still rely on during the outage.

noiseExamples: a viewer emailing about last week's forecast
a spotter whose radio check is garbled
a vendor asking about a software license
a request for a school speaking visit
pressureExamples: a county emergency manager asking whether to sound the sirens now
a TV station asking for a live interview during a warning
a viral post claiming a tornado has touched down in a town the storm has not reached
a county commissioner demanding to know why the warning came late
a utility asking for the likeliest time of damaging winds
an airport asking whether to keep the ramp open
